cases.question: Explain reflection at a spherical mirror and show how the pole, principal axis, focus, normal, incident ray, and reflected ray are related.
A concave mirror has focal length 15 cm and an object is 20 cm in front of it. Locate and classify the image with a principal-ray diagram.
An object is 10 cm from a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Determine the virtual image position and magnification, and construct the backward ray extensions.
Explain refraction from air into glass with a plane interface, a normal, and angle marks showing why the ray bends toward the normal.
A ray in air strikes glass of refractive index 1.5 at 30 degrees. Find the refracted angle and draw the verified incident-normal-refracted chain.
A point object is 30 cm from a spherical air-glass interface of radius 10 cm, with glass index 1.5. Locate the paraxial image and show the surface normal construction.
Explain image formation by a thin converging lens using the optical axis, two focal points, an object, and two principal rays.
An object is 30 cm from a convex lens of focal length 20 cm. Find image distance and magnification and construct the image from two rays.
A biconvex glass lens of index 1.5 has radii plus 20 cm and minus 20 cm in air. Find its focal length and power, and identify both refracting surfaces.
Explain total internal reflection at a dense-to-rare interface by comparing a refracted ray below the critical angle with a reflected ray above it.
Find the critical angle for glass of refractive index 1.5 against air and illustrate the grazing refracted ray at the limiting incidence.
An optical fibre has core index 1.50 and cladding index 1.48 in air. Calculate numerical aperture and acceptance angle and trace a guided meridional ray.
Explain positive and negative linear magnification and relate image height to object height using a clear object-image axis view.
A thin lens has focal length 25 cm. Find its optical power in dioptres and show whether it is converging or diverging.
A real image is formed 60 cm from a lens for an object 30 cm away. Find the signed linear magnification and show the relative object and image heights.
Explain why thin lenses in contact add optical powers and draw their coincident optical-axis arrangement without inventing separation.
Two thin lenses of powers plus 2 D and plus 3 D are in contact. Find equivalent power and focal length and show the common optical axis.
Lenses of powers plus 5 D, minus 2 D, and plus 1 D are in contact. Find the equivalent focal length and classify the combination.
Explain refraction through a prism using both face normals, the internal path, apex angle, and total deviation without guessing ray intersections.
A prism of apex angle 60 degrees and index square root of 3 is at minimum deviation. Find all ray angles and draw the symmetric path.
A 60 degree prism of refractive index 1.5 is adjusted for minimum deviation. Calculate the deviation and incidence and verify path symmetry.
Explain the objective and eyepiece stages of a compound microscope and an astronomical telescope with separate, ordered image planes.
A compound microscope in normal adjustment has tube length 16 cm, objective focal length 4 mm, and eyepiece focal length 2.5 cm. Find magnifying power.
An astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has objective focal length 1.2 m and eyepiece focal length 2 cm. Find angular magnification and show parallel emergent rays.
Explain Huygens principle using a plane wavefront, secondary wavelets, their forward envelope, and normals indicating propagation direction.
A light wavefront travels for 2 ns in vacuum. Find the advance of the wavefront and illustrate equally spaced initial and final fronts.
A sound wavefront advances for 5 ms at 340 m per second. Find its displacement and compare the envelopes from plane and point sources.
Derive the law of reflection from Huygens construction using incident and reflected wavefronts, equal travel distances, and their normals.
A plane wavefront is incident at 35 degrees on a reflector. Use Huygens construction to find and verify the reflected angle.
A wave enters a medium where speed changes from 3 times 10 power 8 to 2 times 10 power 8 m per second at 45 degrees. Derive the refracted angle by Huygens construction.
Explain Young double-slit interference with coherent slits, path difference to a screen point, central maximum, and equally spaced fringes.
In Young experiment, wavelength is 600 nm, screen distance is 2 m, and slit separation is 0.5 mm. Find fringe width and draw the setup.
For the same Young setup with wavelength 600 nm, screen distance 2 m, and slit separation 0.5 mm, locate the third bright fringe and show path difference.
Explain why equal frequency and stable phase difference are required for sustained interference, contrasting coherent and drifting sources.
Two coherent paths differ by 0.75 micrometre for wavelength 0.50 micrometre. Find their phase difference and identify the interference condition.
A phase-locked pair has path difference 1.25 micrometres at wavelength 0.50 micrometre. Calculate phase difference and classify the resulting fringe.
Explain single-slit diffraction with the slit, secondary wavelets, the broad central maximum, and narrower side maxima on a screen.
Light of wavelength 500 nm passes through a 0.20 mm slit onto a screen 2 m away. Find the angular and linear width of the central maximum.
A 0.10 mm slit is illuminated by 600 nm light and observed 1.5 m away. Find the central maximum width and mark its first minima.
Explain the Rayleigh criterion by comparing unresolved and just-resolved diffraction patterns for a circular aperture.
A telescope of aperture 10 cm observes light of wavelength 550 nm. Find its diffraction-limited angular resolution and resolving power.
A microscope uses wavelength 550 nm with numerical aperture 1.4. Find the minimum resolvable separation and illustrate two just-resolved points.
Explain unpolarised and plane-polarised light using transverse field directions, a polarizer axis, and an analyzer axis.
Find Brewster angle for light incident from air onto glass of refractive index 1.5 and show that reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular.
Plane-polarised light of intensity 100 units passes through an analyzer at 60 degrees. Use Malus law to find transmitted intensity and show both axes.
